lead: The Thirteenth Sunday of Year B is about life stronger than death. The Book of Wisdom says plainly that God did not make death: he created all things to exist, and made us for incorruption. In the Gospel Mark weaves two stories into one: a woman who has bled for twelve years touches Jesus’ cloak and is healed, and the twelve-year-old daughter of Jairus, already dead, hears Jesus say, “Talitha cum,” and gets up. Psalm 30 gives thanks: “O Lord, you brought up my soul from Sheol.”

Between them St Paul asks the Corinthians to give generously to the poor church in Jerusalem, because Christ, though rich, became poor for our sake. The link is the same: the God of life gives himself, and those who receive life are called to share it.

set: The Book of Wisdom was written in Greek, probably in Alexandria in Egypt, during the century before Christ. Its author speaks in the person of Solomon, the wise king, but he writes for Jews living among Greeks, who were tempted to give up their faith. It is one of the latest books of the Old Testament, and it is part of the Catholic canon of Scripture.

Chapters 1–5 contrast the righteous and the ungodly. In chapter 2 the ungodly say that life is short, death is the end, so let us enjoy ourselves and crush the righteous man who rebukes us. The author answers that they are wrong about God and about death. Today’s verses come from the opening and from the answer.
str: 1:13: God did not make death and does not delight in it.
1:14: he created all things to exist; creation is wholesome; Hades has no rule on earth.
2:23: God created us for incorruption, in the image of his own eternity.
2:24: death entered through the devil’s envy, and those who belong to him experience it.
kw: Not decaying, not perishing. The word is used by St Paul for the resurrection body: “what is sown is perishable, what is raised is imperishable” (1 Corinthians 15:42).
“Righteousness is immortal” (1:15). Wisdom teaches that the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God (3:1). Life with God does not end at death.

The book says that death entered the world through the devil’s envy (2:24). Envy cannot bear another’s good. Many interpreters see here the serpent of Genesis 3, envious of the human beings made in God’s image.
vv: because God did not make death, and he does not delight in the death of the living.
A strong and simple statement. Death in its full sense, the death that separates from God, is not God’s work. Ezekiel had said the same: God has no pleasure in the death of anyone (Ezekiel 18:32).
For he created all things so that they might exist;
God’s will in creating is that things should be. Creation is good, as Genesis 1 repeats.
for God created us for incorruption, and made us in the image of his own eternity,
An echo of Genesis 1:27. Some Greek manuscripts read “image of his own nature” instead of “eternity”; both readings say that we are made to share God’s life.
but through the devil’s envy death entered the world,

This is one of the first texts in Scripture to link the serpent of Genesis with the devil. The Book of Revelation will call him “that ancient serpent, who is called the Devil and Satan” (Revelation 12:9).
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses: “God did not make death, and he does not delight in the death of the living… It was through the devil’s envy that death entered the world” (CCC 413). It teaches that death is a consequence of sin, and that God had destined man not to die (CCC 1008). It also teaches that behind the disobedience of our first parents lurks a seductive voice opposed to God, the fallen angel called Satan or the devil (CCC 391). The Church does not deny that the body dies according to nature; she proclaims that Christ has conquered death, and that the resurrection of the body is the fulfilment of the incorruption for which we were made.

r.h: Rich, yet for your sakes he became poor
set: Paul is organising a collection among his Gentile churches for the poor Christians of Jerusalem (compare Romans 15:25–27; Galatians 2:10). For him it is more than charity: it is a sign of the unity of Jewish and Gentile believers in one Church. The Corinthians had begun eagerly a year before but had not finished.
In chapters 8–9 Paul encourages them. He points to the churches of Macedonia, poor themselves, who gave beyond their means (8:1–5). Then he points to Christ.
str: v. 7: you excel in everything; excel also in this generous undertaking.
v. 9: the generous act of the Lord Jesus Christ: rich, he became poor, to make you rich.
vv. 13–14: not relief for others and pressure on you, but a fair balance.
v. 15: the manna: “The one who had much did not have too much, and the one who had little did not have too little.”
kw: Paul plays on this word through the chapter. The collection is a charis (v. 7, “generous undertaking”), and Christ’s self-giving is the charis of the Lord (v. 9, “generous act”). Our giving is a share in his grace.
He became a beggar, one who has nothing. Paul thinks of the whole mystery of the Son becoming man, as in Philippians 2:6–8.
Equality, fairness. Paul does not ask the Corinthians to become poor so that others may be rich; he asks for a balance in which abundance meets need.
vv: so we want you to excel also in this generous undertaking.
Paul does not command; he invites. Generosity is to be one more of the gifts in which the community shines.
though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich.
One of the great Christ verses of the New Testament. The riches are the divine life; the poverty is his birth, his life and his Cross. The exchange is all to our advantage.
your present abundance and their need,
Today one community has more, tomorrow another. The Church is one body in which goods circulate.
The one who had much did not have too much, and the one who had little did not have too little.
Paul quotes Exodus 16:18. In the desert God gave manna to each according to need. Sharing in the Church is meant to reflect that divine providence.
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse when it teaches that the whole life of Christ is a mystery of redemption: by becoming poor he enriches us with his poverty (CCC 517). In its teaching on love for the poor it quotes St John Chrysostom: not to enable the poor to share in our goods is to steal from them and deprive them of life; the goods we possess are not ours, but theirs (CCC 2446). The collection at Mass, and the gifts given for the poor and for needy dioceses, continue Paul’s collection. They are not a tax but a share in the grace of Christ.

set: Jesus has just crossed back from the Gentile side of the lake, where he healed the man with the legion of demons (5:1–20). In chapters 4–5 Mark shows his power over the storm, the demons, sickness and death.

Mark often places one story inside another, so that each explains the other. Here the story of Jairus is interrupted by the woman with the haemorrhage. Both are called “daughter”, both involve the number twelve, and both turn on faith and touch. The shorter form of the reading keeps only Jairus’ story.
str: vv. 21–24: Jairus, a leader of the synagogue, begs Jesus to come to his dying daughter.
vv. 25–29: the woman who had suffered twelve years touches his cloak and is healed.
vv. 30–34: “Who touched my clothes?” She tells the whole truth. “Daughter, your faith has made you well.”
vv. 35–36: news of the girl’s death; “Do not fear, only believe.”
vv. 37–40: with Peter, James and John to the house; the mourners laugh.
vv. 41–43: “Talitha cum”; the girl gets up; give her something to eat.
kw: A respected lay leader who arranged the services. Jairus is an important man, yet he falls at Jesus’ feet. Grief and love make him humble.

Mark uses the same verb for healing and for salvation: Jairus asks that his daughter be “made well” (v. 23); the woman thinks “I will be made well” (v. 28); Jesus says “your faith has made you well” (v. 34). Bodily healing points to the salvation of the whole person.
Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke, kept by Mark and translated for his Greek readers: “Little girl, get up!” Many later manuscripts have the longer form koumi; the oldest have koum.
vv: My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be made well, and live.
A father’s prayer, urgent and full of faith. He believes that Jesus’ touch can give life.
If I but touch his clothes, I will be made well.

The law of Leviticus 15 meant that her bleeding made her ritually unclean, and for twelve years she had lived with that and with her illness. She comes from behind, quietly. Her faith is real, though still timid.
Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your disease.
Jesus will not let her slip away unseen. He calls her “daughter”, gives her peace, and confirms her healing before everyone. She is healed in body and restored in dignity.
Do not fear, only believe.
The word to Jairus is the word to every Christian in the face of death. Faith is asked for precisely when there seems nothing more to hope.
Talitha cum,
Jesus takes her by the hand. The verb “get up” is the same family of words used for the resurrection. The early Church heard in this a sign of the resurrection of all who belong to Christ.
ch: The Catechism lists the raising of Jairus’ daughter with that of the young man of Nain and of Lazarus as signs announcing Christ’s own Resurrection (CCC 994). It notes that Jesus hears the prayer of faith expressed in deeds, such as the woman who touches his clothes (CCC 2616), and that the sick try to touch him, for power comes from him and heals (CCC 1504). In the sacraments Christ continues to touch us: “power came forth from him” then, and it comes forth now in Baptism, the Eucharist and the Anointing of the Sick. The command to give the girl something to eat shows his care for ordinary needs, and the Church has often heard in it an echo of the food of life she gives her children.

qa: If God did not make death, why do we die?

The Church teaches that death entered as a consequence of sin (CCC 1008), not as part of God’s first plan. The body dies according to nature, but for those who are in Christ death has been changed: it becomes a passage to life with God. Christ did not take death away from this world; he went through it and opened the way to the resurrection.
Was the woman superstitious to think that touching his clothes would heal her?

Her faith was imperfect, perhaps mixed with ideas of magic, but Jesus accepted it and led it further. He calls her forward so that her trust in his clothes becomes a personal meeting with him. The Church honours relics and holy objects in the same spirit: never as magic, always as a way to the person of Christ and the saints.
Why does Paul ask for money in a letter that is Scripture?

Because love for the poor belongs to the heart of the Gospel. Paul’s collection was also a sign of unity between Gentile and Jewish Christians. He asks gently, without command, and he roots it in Christ’s own self-giving. Giving for the poor is part of worship, not a separate matter.
rite: In the Roman Rite the Thirteenth Sunday of Year B joins healing, resurrection and charity. Peter’s Pence, the gift of the faithful to the Holy Father for his works of charity, is traditionally linked with the solemnity of Saints Peter and Paul on Tuesday. Today is also a good day to pray for the sick of the parish and to bring them Holy Communion.
study: Wisdom says “God did not make death.” How does this change the way I think about illness, ageing and the death of those I love?
Paul says Christ became poor to make us rich. In what concrete way can my family share our “abundance” with someone in need this week?
The woman came from behind; Jesus called her forward. Is there something I bring to God quietly that he wants me to bring openly, perhaps in confession?
Jesus said to Jairus, “Do not fear, only believe.” Where do I need to hear that word today?
